Write an item model for automatic item generation

Source: R/ai-aig.R
item_model.Rd

An item model (Gierl & Haladyna, 2013) is a parent item with variable elements: A stem, a key and distractors written as templates, the values each variable can take, and constraints that every generated item must meet. generate_isomorphs() fills the templates to produce isomorphs: Items that test the same thing in the same way and differ only in their surface. This is the classical, template-based route to automatic item generation (AIG); it is deterministic and every item can be traced to its values. generate_items() is the language-model route.

Usage

item_model(
  stem,
  key,
  distractors,
  values,
  constraints = NULL,
  name = "M",
  digits = 2
)

Arguments

stem

the stem template.

key

the template of the correct answer.

distractors

a character vector of distractor templates, one per wrong option. Name them to record the misconception behind each.

values

a named list with the values each variable can take.

constraints

optional character vector of R expressions of the variables, each of which must be TRUE for a combination of values to be used.

name

a short name for the item model, used in item ids.

digits

largest number of decimals printed for computed values.

Value

An object of class mv_item_model. Print it to see the templates and how many isomorphs it can generate.

Details

Templates mark variable parts with braces. Inside the braces is any R expression of the variables, so "{l}" inserts the value of l and "{2 * (l + w)}" inserts the computed perimeter. Whole numbers are printed without decimals and with a thousands separator, other numbers with up to digits decimals. Two helpers can be used in templates: money(x) prints $12.50, and fmt(x, d) prints x with exactly d decimals.

Write each distractor from a misconception: The answer a student with a specific misunderstanding would give, such as the area for the perimeter. Write constraints for what the values must satisfy (for example that a result is a whole number), and to keep the distractors different from the key and from each other for every combination of values.

References

Gierl, M. J., & Haladyna, T. M. (Eds.). (2013). Automatic item generation: Theory and practice. Routledge.

See also

generate_isomorphs() to generate items, calibrate_families() to check after field testing that the isomorphs are equally difficult; the AI Hub.

Examples

perimeter <- item_model(
  stem = "A garden is {l} m long and {w} m wide. What is its perimeter?",
  key = "{2 * (l + w)} m",
  distractors = c(area = "{l * w} m", one_length_one_width = "{l + w} m",
                  two_lengths_only = "{2 * l + w} m"),
  values = list(l = 5:15, w = 2:9),
  constraints = "l > w",
  name = "PER")
perimeter
#> <mv_item_model> PER
#>   Stem: A garden is {l} m long and {w} m wide. What is its perimeter?
#>   Key:  {2 * (l + w)} m
#>   Distractor 1: {l * w} m  (area)
#>   Distractor 2: {l + w} m  (one length one width)
#>   Distractor 3: {2 * l + w} m  (two lengths only)
#>   l: 5, 6, 7, ..., 14, 15
#>   w: 2, 3, 4, ..., 8, 9
#>   Constraints: l > w 
#>   73 combinations of values meet the constraints; 72 give items whose options all differ.
generate_isomorphs(perimeter, n = 3)
#> PER: 1 of 73 combinations of values give two identical options or cannot be computed, and were left out. Add a constraint to rule them out.
#> # A tibble: 3 × 11
#>   id     model stem              A     B     C     D     key       l     w flag 
#>   <chr>  <chr> <chr>             <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <int> <int> <chr>
#> 1 PER-01 PER   A garden is 5 m … 10 m  14 m  7 m   12 m  B         5     2 ""   
#> 2 PER-02 PER   A garden is 12 m… 60 m  29 m  34 m  17 m  C        12     5 ""   
#> 3 PER-03 PER   A garden is 11 m… 40 m  31 m  20 m  99 m  A        11     9 ""
